evidence.source: Instagram, Rewarding original creators on Instagram (read by the build session)
evidence.finding: adding only a border, a watermark, subtitles or a credit in the caption to someone else's work is not original; accounts that mostly repost are no longer recommended; judged over a rolling 30 days. The page says nothing about a creator's own video on several platforms

evidence.source: v12 build, batch V2c-b2a (the platforms)
evidence.finding: found by reading the code: an approved Short would have been posted under the special reels' text (a courtroom, a wrong cadence, an ask), and one text went to all three platforms; both are gone - the texts are built per platform and a test reads them

items.title: What something IS goes into a field of its own; where it stands goes into its status - never read one for the other
items.summary: Whether a Short was made was read out of a status text, and 'HELD' meant two things on one tab: a Short paid in full once read as not made. Now 'made' is a field of the record (with the hash of the file), handing a Short to Publishing is a record too, and no code decides anything from a status word. A Short made while uploads are closed keeps its file in Drive and goes out when they open.

evidence.source: v12 build, batch V2c-b2a (the platforms)
evidence.finding: found by reading the code: a Short made while uploads were not confirmed open was counted as made and its file was nowhere - it could never be posted; the first draft of this batch's own pass read a status prefix again and was changed to a record before any test ran

items.title: V2c-b2a build takeaway: write the break list before the last test run - it finds what a green test hides
items.summary: The list of deliberate breaks, written as 'what would fail if this line went?', found a check that could pass a Short which never reached YouTube - its test was green for another reason - and three missing tests, before one break ran. And the sweep had never published a Short: a proof that does not walk the new path proves the old one.

evidence.source: v12 build, batch V2c-b2a (the platforms)
evidence.finding: 63 deliberate one-line breaks of the release path each failed at least one test. Before they ran, the list showed that 'not connected' excused YouTube too in check release_sheet while its test failed for an Instagram row left waiting a line earlier; and that three guards had no test (a repair the platform accepts and does not apply, a second pass over a record that already has a platform id, the tick's hook).

evidence.source: v12 build, batch V2c-b2a (the platforms), reading the upload path
evidence.finding: Found by reading, not by a test: an approved Short would have been posted under the special reels' text; a Short made while uploads were closed lost its file; a second pass would have posted a Reel twice; a job cut off after an upload would have uploaded again; the sweep made its Shorts with publish off. Only an offline stand-in has answered so far: no real platform has met the release sheet.

items.title: A long video about a promoted Short opens on that Short's own footage, laid by code under its first sentences
items.summary: The pictures real viewers stayed for open the long video: the Short's clips in its order, at the speed they were shown, without the loop, under the long video's own voice; the first line is the Short's first sentence. Three animated scenes are bought for the rest. A video that would open with other pictures is held before any picture is paid; under an override it opens on its own promise scene.

evidence.source: YouTube Help 9314415, Measure key moments for audience retention (read by the build session)
evidence.finding: 'Intro tells you what percentage of your audience still watched your video after the first 30 seconds'; a high figure could mean the first 30 seconds 'matched the viewer's expectation of the video's thumbnail and title'

evidence.source: v12 build, batch V2c-b2b1 (the opening)
evidence.finding: in every offline run the long video of a promoted Short opened on 14 to 17 seconds of that Short's footage (5 to 6 shots from 3 clips), three scenes were bought instead of four and no hook lab was run; a production whose archive was gone was held before any picture was paid

items.title: An upright clip in a wide frame: one picture, its own blurred copy as the ground, as wide as its sharpness allows
items.summary: YouTube tested three ways to show an upright video on a wide screen: empty sides lost, several videos side by side strayed from one video at a time, one video on a blurred background of its own colours won. So the opening window is one dial from the whole clip to the filled frame; its width follows the clip's measured pixels and a limit on how far a paid picture may be enlarged.

evidence.source: YouTube Official Blog, A design journey from mobile to TV: YouTube Shorts arrive on the big screen (read by the build session)
evidence.finding: the plain player: 'the joy of Shorts gets lost'; several at once 'strayed too far from the essence of Shorts', which 'features one video at a time'; the chosen design has 'a color-sampled blurred background' and testers preferred it

evidence.source: Google Research, AutoFlip: an open source framework for intelligent video reframing (read by the build session)
evidence.finding: static cropping 'often lead[s] to unsatisfactory results'; when the important content cannot fit, the frame is padded with 'a blurred version of the original frame'

items.title: The hero clip model has no field for the shape or the pixel size of a clip: it follows the start picture
items.summary: The clip model's inputs are a start picture, an optional end picture, the prompt and a length of 3 to 15 seconds. Nothing sets the shape or the size: a Short's clips are upright because their start pictures are, and the same scene in a wide frame would be a second paid clip and a new draw. Its page states no pixel size, so every clip is measured on the file before it is used.

evidence.source: fal, the hero clip model's page and API schema (read by the build session)
evidence.finding: inputs: image_url, end_image_url, prompt or multi_prompt, duration 3 to 15 seconds (default 5), generate_audio, shot_type; no aspect or resolution field; USD 0.084 a second with audio off

items.title: To prove that a finished film shows a clip, compare the detail of both frames, never a hash of a tiny copy
items.summary: A difference hash of a 9 by 8 grey copy follows a vignette on a smooth picture: under the trial's grade it called the film's own footage 22 to 26 of 64 points different. The correlation of detail - each small grey copy minus its own blur - drops brightness, tint and vignette: 0.80 to 0.93 for the same footage, under 0.1 for other pictures. A footage frame without detail is not judged.

evidence.source: N. Krawetz, Kind of Like That (read by the build session)
evidence.finding: the difference hash 'won't change if the image is scaled or the aspect ratio changes'; a distance above 10 of 64 bits is 'likely a different image'

evidence.source: v12 build, batch V2c-b2b1 (the opening)
evidence.finding: 12 frames of a finished offline film against the footage they show: the difference hash differed in 11 to 26 of 64 points (limit 12) under the trial's vignette, grain and stamp; the correlation of detail gave 0.80 to 0.93, and -0.07 to 0.10 against other pictures

items.title: The channel's own footage in a new video is not what the reuse rules name; as a second short upload it would be
items.summary: YouTube's reused-content rule names content 'already on YouTube or another online source' taken without significant change; its repetition rule allows the same intro across videos whose bulk differs. Neither speaks of a creator's own footage in a new video: the channel's own Short under a new narration is safe ground. As a cut-down it would be the Short again, so no footage shot is offered to one.

evidence.source: YouTube Help 1311392, YouTube channel monetization policies (read by the build session)
evidence.finding: reused content: repurposing content 'already on YouTube or another online source without adding significant original commentary, substantive modifications, or educational or entertainment value'; allowed: 'Same intro and outro for your videos, but the bulk of your content is different'
